## Proof

We determine the set of continuous group homomorphisms $f \colon \hat{\mathbb{Z}} \to \mathbb{Z}$, where $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$ carries its profinite (compact Hausdorff) topology and $\mathbb{Z}$ carries its usual topology as a topological group, which is the **discrete** topology.

**Key facts.**

1. $\hat{\mathbb{Z}} = \varprojlim_n \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is a profinite group, hence **compact** (and Hausdorff).
2. $\mathbb{Z}$ with its usual topology is **discrete** (every singleton is open), hence Hausdorff, and its compact subsets are exactly the **finite** subsets.

**Argument.**

Let $f \colon \hat{\mathbb{Z}} \to \mathbb{Z}$ be a continuous group homomorphism. Since $f$ is continuous and $\hat{\mathbb{Z}}$ is compact, the image
$$f(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$$
is a compact subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ (continuous image of a compact set is compact). Because $\mathbb{Z}$ is discrete, every compact subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ is finite. Hence $f(\hat{\mathbb{Z}})$ is a **finite** subset of $\mathbb{Z}$.

But $f(\hat{\mathbb{Z}})$ is also a **subgroup** of $\mathbb{Z}$ (image of a group homomorphism). The only finite subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the trivial subgroup $\{0\}$: indeed, any nonzero $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ generates the infinite cyclic subgroup $k\mathbb{Z}$, which is infinite.

Therefore $f(\hat{\mathbb{Z}}) = \{0\}$, i.e., $f$ is the trivial (zero) homomorphism.

**Conclusion.**

The trivial homomorphism is certainly continuous, so it belongs to the set. By the argument above, it is the **only** continuous homomorphism. Hence

$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cts}}\!\big(\hat{\mathbb{Z}},\, \mathbb{Z}\big) \;=\; \{0\},$$

the set consisting of the single trivial homomorphism.

### PROOF COMPLETE
